doc.title: Clyde Kerr Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 22, 2006

title: Forty-two years of teaching, versatility, and father's Saturday workshops
summary: He just retired after 42 years teaching, worked in street bands, clubs, symphony and Broadway, and recalls his father's workshops in their shotgun house from 1947.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Uh huh. Don’t forget about the music. That’s well said. I suspect that you’ve worn a lot of hats in the music business to make a living you have to prepared to do a lot of different things.
Oh definitely yes. Oh yeah. If you want to work and do — you know I taught school for 42 years. I just retired last week, 42 years.

When I started man, after the first couple of weeks, I said I will never make ten years doing this. So 42 years later here I am just retiring. So I taught. My father was a teacher and my grandfather and my grandmother were teachers. My sister is a teacher and my daughters. One is still a teacher. One taught for three years and she gave it up, she is now a nurse. But playing music, I started out I just wanted to be just strictly a jazz musician but like most New Orleans musicians who wanted to just play jazz you have to play the rock & roll or rhythm & blues or brass bands, so I’ve done all that. I played in the street, I played in the clubs, I played in the symphony halls, I played Broadway shows. My degree is in music education. So trying to be say a complete musician, knowing how to read music, I was able to do things that curtailed reading music and playing in bands or orchestras or whatever, as well as going on gigs when there’s no written music at all. So by being able to do that I was able to do a lot of different things which has helped me in some way to be the type of teacher that I turned out to be, to experience all those different things. That’s what I brought to my lessons, classrooms, you know. And I was very fortunate because I grew up in the home where my father was actually a musician and a teacher, and as a kid I can remember that — I was born in 1943 — I can remember as far back as 1947 on Saturdays my father would have workshops in the living room of our home. And we had a small shotgun house, you know, straight, you know the shotgun. So we had to take out all the furniture in the living room, put it in the alleyway, so these 30 to 35 musicians could get in there and play. And man that was a big novelty for me as a kid just watching all those musicians, all those trumpets, saxophones, trombone players, on Saturday.
